EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 125 
December 28, 1920. 
Mr. Ernest D. Pickell may be appointed to the position of rural free delivery 
carrier at Huron, S. Dak., without regard to civil-service examination. 
This order is issued on the recommendation of the Postmaster General on 
account of this employee’s faithful and efficient service, and because of the 
difficulty experienced in securing a permanent rural carrier to fill this position. 
His appeintment would be in the interest of the service. He is disqualified 
from taking the required examination on account of his age, he being 52 years 
old. 
January 28, 1921. 
Mrs. Emma V. Morgan may be appointed to a position in the classified service 
in the Department of Labor without reference to the requirements of the civil￾service rules. , 
This order is recommended by the Secretary of Labor, who states that Mrs. 
Morgan is a woman of very unusual ability, efficiency, and reliability. 
February 2, 1921. 
Morris A. Parris may be appointed as clerk to act as confidential secretary 
to the Director of the Bureau of Standards, at $1,800 per annum, without re￾gard to the requirements of the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Director of the Bureau 
of Standards and of the Secretary of Commerce, Mr. Parris having demon￾strated under temporary appointment that he possesses the peculiar qualifica￾tions and experience necessary for the duties of the position. 
February 10, 1921. 
Mr. Arthur Byrd may be appointed a clerk in the Navy Department without 
compliance with the civil-service rules. 
This order is issued in view of the long and efficient service Mr. Byrd has 
rendered in the Navy Department. His duties and responsibilities compare 
favorably with those of many clerks. The position which Mr. Byrd fills has 
grown to one of such importance that if his service were terminated for any 
cause it would be necessary to replace him with a clerk. 
February 12, 1921. 
Mrs. May G. Pollock, of Illinois, may be appointed in the classified service 
without regard to civil-service rules. 
NoTeE.—The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of 
the above order. 
February 18, 1921. 
Miss Margaret Reardon, of virginia, and Mr. Joseph F. Murphy, of New Jer￾sey, may be appointed to positions in the classified service of the Government 
without reference to the civil-service rules. 
Miss Reardon and Mr. Murphy have been employed in the executive office for 
a number of months and have rendered efficient service. 
March 4, 1921. 
Miller W. Gieseking, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a clerical posi￾tion in the classified service of the Government without reference to the civil￾service rules. ; 
Mr. Gieseking has been employed in the executive offices for nearly three 
vears and has rendered efficient and faithful service. 
March 5, 1921. 
Mrs. Mabel P. LeRoy, of Michigan, appointed by the Secretary of the Interior 
February 25, 1910, to the position of clerk to sign land patents, is hereby desig￾nated as required by law to sign said patents. 
Note.—The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of 
the above order. 
March 19, 1921. 
Mrs. Mary T. K. McBlair, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to a 
position in the classified civil service without reference to the civil-service rules. 
Mrs. McBlair has been temporarily employed in the Bureau of Naturalization 
in the Department of Labor, where she has rendered faithful and industrious 
service.

AUTHORITY TO EXTEND, FOR SINGLE PERIODS OF A YEAR OR LESS, THE EMPLOYMENTS 
OF PERSONS ENGAGED ON ACTIVITIES GROWING OUT OF THE RECENT WAR. 
- May 21, 1921. 
Subject to the restrictive conditions herein named, the Civil Service Commis￾sion is hereby authorized to extend for single periods of a year or less the 
employments of qualified persons engaged on activities growing out of the recent 
war, which are temporary and diminishing in their nature, such as salvage 
boards, claims boards, sales organizations, ete. This order is to apply only to 
cases of persons whose temporary appointments have been authorized by the 
commission, and will permit continuance only in the class of work for which 
originally appo’nted, and will not confer any rights of transfer, promotion, or 
assignment to classified positions. 
EXTENSION OF ELIGIBILITY FOR REINSTATEMENT OR APPOINTMENT OF PERSONS FOR￾MERLY IN THE CLASSIFIED SERVICE WHO SERVED WITH ORGANIZATIONS DOING 
DISTINCTIVE WAR SERVICE. 
May 31, 1921. 
In the discretion of the Civil Service Commission, the time during which 
persons formerly in the competitive classified service served with organiza￾tions doing distinctive war service shall not count against their period of 
eligibility under civil-service Rule IX for reinstatement, nor against their 
eligibility under civil-service Rule X for transfer, provided they have had 
continuous service. 
WAIVER OF MAXIMUM AGE LIMIT FOR PRESIDENTIAL POSTMASTER, EVERETT, WASH. 
July 21, 1921. 
The maximum age limit in the examination for postmaster at Everett, Wash., 
is hereby waived. This is done especially for the purpose of permitting ap- plicants to take the exam’'nation who have had long experience as postmaster 
and who are believed to be especially efficient, and is done on the recommenda￾tion of the Postmaster General for the good of the service. 
REMOVING POSITION OF FEMALE CLERK, DESIGNATED BY PRESIDENT TO SIGN LAND 
PATENTS, FROM COMPETITIVE SERVICE, 
July 27, 1921. 
Executive order of January 27, 1913, .placing the position of female clerk 
to be designated by the President to sign land patents, $1,200, in the competi-* 
tive classified service, is hereby revoked. 
MAXIMUM AGE LIMIT, PRESIDENTIAL POSTMASTER. 
July 27, 1921. 
The Executive order of May 10, 1921, prescribing examinations for the 
appointment of presidential postmasters, is hereby amended by striking out in - 
the second paragraph the words “ such vacancy ” and substituting therefor the 
words ‘“ the date of examination.” As amended, the paragraph will read: 
“No person who has passed his sixty-fifth birthday, or who has not actually 
resided within the delivery of such office for two years next preceding the date 
of examination shall be given the examination herein provided for.” 
APPOINTMENTS IN EMPLOYMENT SERVICE WITHOUT REGARD TO CIVIL-SERVICE ACT 
AND RULES. 
September 30, 1921. 
The Secretary of Labor is authorized to make appointments to the various 
positions in the Employment Service without regard to the civil-service act and rules, 
This order is recommended by the Secretary of Labor.

“ When a vacancy exists or hereafter occurs in the position of postmaster at

work who are in classified service. All of these are under the permanent pro￾visions of the civil service law and rules. ; 
These permanent rules provide for the certification of the highest three 
eligibles, from which list of three each necessary appointment is made. The 
successful operation of the principles of civil service law has demonstrated the 
wisdom of. this provision. This leaves in the appointing power, who has the 
ultimate responsibility for efficient administration, the necessary, constitutional 
right of choice. This right of selection is the kind of responsibility which can 
not legally be and is not abridged by act of Congress, @nd is in exact harmony 
with the spirit of the civil service principle.

are now under such civil-service laws and regulations as bring them within the 
privileges and conditions of the classified service.

measured by. the requirements of progress, and is one which I hope will be 
made. Under existing laws the Executive has no power to require that these 
offices be placed in the classified service.

ORDERS RELATING TO THE RETIREMENT ACT OF MAY 22, 1920. 
EXTENSION OF THE PROVISIONS OF THE ACT TO INCLUDE CERTAIN GROUPS OF EM￾PLOYEES IN THE EXECUTIVE CIVIL SERVICE. 
June 7, 1922. 
1. Under authority conferred by section 1 of the act of May 22, 1920, for 
the retirement of employees in the classified civil service, and for other pur￾poses, and upon recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, the provisions 
of said act are hereby extended, effective September 1, 1922, to include groups 
of employees in the executive civil service as follows: : 
(a) Unclassified laborers in all cities and in establishments or offices in 
which appointments are made under labor regulations approved by the Presi￾dent. 
(b) Unclassified laborers in all offices in which appointments are made from 
subclerical or other registers for the classified service. 
(¢) Unclassified laborers who have been transferred from classified positions. 
2. An employee to whom this extension applies shall, in order to receive 
credit for service rendered since August 1, 1920, deposit with the Treasurer of 
the United States an amount equivalent to such deductions, with interest, as 
would have been made from his salary, pay, or compensation during such period 
had he been subject to the act; but failure to make such deposit shall not 
deprive the employee of credit for service to which he would otherwise be en￾titled. 
3. The provisions of this Executive order shall not extend to unclassified 
laborers employed in parts of the service in which classified employees have 
been excluded from the provisions of the retirement act by Executive order 
under section 1 of the act, nor shall they apply to employees who are in receipt 
of basic salary, pay, or compensation at a rate less than $600 per annum. 
4. The Ixecutive orders of May 24, 1922, transferring eight unclassified 
employees in the office of the Superintendent of the State, War and Navy 
Department Buildings to the classified service are hereby revoked. 
August 2, 1922. 
By authority contained in section 1 of an act for the retirement of employees 
in the classified civil service, and for other purposes, approved May 22, 1920, 
and upon recommendation of the Director of the Coast and Geodetic Survey, 
the Secretary of Commerce, and the Civil Service Commission, junior engineers 
and deck officers of the Coast and Geodetic Survey are hereby excluded from 
the operation of said act. 
Although these employees are appointed through competitive examination in 
accordance with the civil service act and rules, and are given a probationary 
appointment, their employment is temporary in the sense that those who are 
retained beyond the probationary period and who show the proper qualifications 
are promoted to the commissioned force of the Bureau and thereafter receive 
the same pay and allowances prescribed for officers of the Navy, and are re￾tired in accordance with the law relating to the retirement of commissioned 
officers in the Navy, while those who do not show the proper qualifications 
for a commissioned officer in the Coast and Geodetic Survey and who are un￾able to pass the required physical examination to establish eligibility for pro￾motion to the commissioned rank are separated from the service. In either 
case, their classified service is tentative and of short duration, and their in￾clusion under the provisions of the retirement act results only in deductions 
for a short period and later reimbursement. 
ORDERS RELATING TO EXAMINATIONS FOR PRESIDENTIAL POST OFFICES.

OFFICES WHO SERVED IN THE WORLD WAR. - 
October 14, 1921.

scope of the civil service law and, therefore, as a matter of law, no * preference ” 
is applicable thereto, yet, in order that those young men and women who 
served in the World War, having their scholastic and business experience in￾tercepted and interrupted thereby, may not suffer any disadvantage in the 
competition for such postmasterships, I direct the Civil Service Commission,

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 155 
(b) A person honorably released from the active military or naval service of the United States after service in the Civil War, War with Spain, or War with Germany, or his widow, or an Army nurse of any war, may be reinstated, if physically qualified, within five years from the date of separation from his unclassified position; or, if a person served in the War with Germany, he may be reinstated within five years from the date of his honorable discharge from the military or naval service. - {e) The widow of a veteran of the War with Germany formerly in the unclassified service, who was the wife of such veteran while he was in the military service, may “be reinstated within five years from the date of cessation of her husband’s military service by death or otherwise without discredit. d) A person separated from an unclassified position in the field service may be reemployed in the same office within one year without certificate. 
ORDERS EXCEPTING PERSONS NAMED FROM THE REQUIREMENTS OF THE RULES. 
November 18, 1922. 
Frank C. Staley has a classified status in the field service of the Veterans’ Bureau under the civil-service law as result of open competitive examination. The require- ment of six months’ service as a classified employee before transfer is hereby waived to permit Mr. Staley’s transfer from the Veterans’ Bureau to the Post Office Depart￾ment. 
December 30, 1922. 
# Mrs. Anna M. Curran may be reappointed as printer’s assistant in the Bureau of Engraving and Printing of the Treasury Department. She served in this position from September 15, 1919, when she was appointed without examination under author- ity of an Executive order of January 15, 1918, until August 13, 1921, when she was furloughed because of reduction of force, her furlough being largely due to the fact that her husband was employed in the Government service. Since her furlough she has been left a widow by the assassination of her husband. She received several bullet wounds in trying to protect him. She has been out of the service too long to be eligible for reemployment, and the Executive order under which she received Shpoigimeit has been revoked. She could have remained in the service indefinitely if no occasion had arisen to require her separation. In view of all the circumstances the Secretary of the Treasury recommends her reinstatement. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation that she be reap- pointed with the same status she would have had if she had remained in the service under her original appointment. 
January 8, 1923. 
Mrs. Frank L. Scott may be appointed to a clerical position in the classified service of the War Department without regard to the civil-service rules. This order is recommended by the Chief of Finance, under whom Mrs. Scott served under temporary appointment. She has performed her duties in a satisfactory manner and by her general aptitude has become a valuable asset to the service. Her husband is confined in St. Elizabeths Hospital suffering from paresis and his recovery is hope- less, this condition doubtless having resulted largely from his service as a soldier in the Tropics and to overwork during the late war. While in the Tropics he contracted a fever, which caused a generally weakened condition of his system. During the war he organized an important unit of the War Department in Washington and gave attention to his work without regard to hours. Mrs. Scott has been left solely upon her own resources, as her husband receives no pension or other remuneration. The Secretary of War, while reluctant to recommend an Executive order, states 
that favorable action will be agreeable to him. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
February 20, 1923. 
Mrs. Mildred L. Jennings may be appointed to a clerical position in the General Accounting Office without regard to the civil-service rules. 
This order is recommended by the Comptroller General, who has known Mrs, Jennings for many years, has supervised her work, and whose services, because of her dependability and qualifications, can be used to advantage on a particular work about which he feels some concern. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending this order. 
February 26, 1923. 
Mr. Thomas S. Shelley may be reinstated with a classified status effective September 7, 1917.

This order is recommended by the Secretary of Labor because of the need on the Mexican border of the services of a man particularly familiar with local conditions and methods in order to secure the administration of the immigration laws on the border as applying to the surreptitious entry of aliens. Captain Hanson was for many years United States marshal for the Southern District of Texas, in which capacity he had charge of 500 miles of the border and as head of and in charge of the ranger forces of the State of Texas he has become thoroughly familiar with the particular problems presented. Because of Captain Hanson’s experience, which peculiarly qualifies him for the duties of the position of immigration inspector on the Mexican border, and because the register of eligibles is depleted the Civil Service Commission joins with the Secre- tary of Labor in recommending this order.
